name: How to Compare Full-House Remodel Bids From Los Angeles General Contractors

mainEntity.name: How can I compare detailed bids from general contractors in Los Angeles for a full-house remodel so I’m not misled by low allowances or missing scope items?
mainEntity.text: How can I compare detailed bids from general contractors in Los Angeles for a full-house remodel so I’m not misled by low allowances or missing scope items?

acceptedAnswer.text: When comparing full-house remodel bids in Los Angeles, the “lowest” price is often based on missing items or unrealistically low allowances. To make fair comparisons, start by creating a **written scope of work** and basic finish schedule (flooring type, cabinet level, countertop material range, plumbing fixture grade). Provide this same document to each contractor. When the proposals arrive, check that each includes permits, required inspections, trash hauling, and clean-up. Confirm whether engineering, Title 24 energy calculations, and city plan-check fees are included or excluded. Look closely at **allowances** for cabinets, tile, plumbing fixtures, and lighting; very low allowances signal that the final price will rise once you pick actual products. Ask each contractor to supply a **line-item breakdown** showing major categories: demolition, framing, plumbing, electrical, HVAC, drywall, finishes, and project management. This reveals where numbers differ and whether scope is missing. Clarify in writing who is responsible for unexpected items like substandard wiring, hidden termite damage, or unpermitted prior work. Finally, evaluate schedule assumptions, warranty terms, and project supervision, not just cost. A detailed, transparent bid is often a better value than a vague low number that will likely grow through change orders.
acceptedAnswer.description: Normalize bids by creating a detailed scope list and finish schedule, then verify each contractor has included the same items and realistic allowances. Watch for missing permits, engineering, clean-up, and utility upgrades, and ask for written clarifications before judging which proposal is truly lower cost.
